name: Grünfeld Defense: Russian System
summary: In the Russian System of the Grünfeld (5.Qb3), White regains the c4-pawn and builds a broad e4/d4 centre that Black tries to undermine.
intro: The Russian System is one of the principal ways to meet the Grünfeld Defence, arising after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Qb3 dxc4 6.Qxc4 O-O 7.e4. White recaptures the pawn with the queen and erects a large pawn centre, while Black adopts the classic Grünfeld strategy of attacking that centre with pieces rather than occupying it. The result is one of the most heavily analysed battlegrounds of the whole opening.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Bg7 Qb3 dxc4 Qxc4 O-O e4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Russian System is defined by White's early queen sortie to b3, which recovers the pawn on c4 and lends immediate support to the central advance e2-e4. Once White has pawns on d4 and e4, the position takes on the essential Grünfeld character: White owns a broad, mobile centre and the space that comes with it, while Black relies on the fianchettoed g7-bishop and a swarm of piece pressure to prove that the centre is a liability rather than an asset. The queen on c4 is actively placed but can also become a target, and much of Black's play is coloured by the tempo-gaining possibilities against it.

Black's counterplay revolves around striking at the base of the centre, most often with ...c5 and sometimes ...b5, prising open lines for the g7-bishop and the queen's rook. A recurring manoeuvre is ...Bg4 followed by ...Nfd7 and ...Nb6, harassing the white queen, trading off a defender of d4 and preparing to hit the centre. If White is allowed to consolidate with a rook on d1 and pieces harmoniously placed, the central pawns become a genuine strength; if Black succeeds in liquidating or blockading them, the long diagonal and the exposed white queen offer excellent chances. The struggle is therefore a race between White's consolidation and Black's dismantling of the centre.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The oldest main line is the Prins Variation with 7...Bg4, when Black immediately pins the f3-knight and follows up with ...Nfd7 and ...Nb6, gaining time on the queen and pressing against d4. White typically answers with Be2 and Be3, meeting the pressure by supporting the centre and preparing to castle. A closely related and highly respected route is 7...a6, the Hungarian Variation, preparing ...b5 to kick the queen and expand on the queenside before committing the other pieces; it has long been a reliable choice for Black at the highest level.

White has several ways to handle the middlegame after the centre is established. The classical set-up with Be2, O-O and Rd1 (often reaching a Be3 configuration) keeps the pawns intact and invites Black to declare his intentions, whereas more ambitious players choose Be3 and Rd1 quickly to bolster d4 against ...c5. Black, for his part, must decide between the ...Bg4 lines and the flexible ...a6/...b5 plans, and between an early ...c5 or a slower build-up with ...Nc6 and ...Rd8. Each choice shades the position toward either a sharp central clash or a more manoeuvring struggle over the fate of the d4- and e4-pawns.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Grünfeld Defence takes its name from the Austrian master Ernst Grünfeld, who employed it in the early 1920s, and it quickly became a leading hypermodern answer to 1.d4 by inviting White to build a centre that Black then attacks. The Russian System, with its early Qb3, was developed and popularised by Soviet analysts in the mid-twentieth century, which is how it acquired its name. It became a mainstay of elite practice and has been contested by many World Champions on both sides of the board, from the classical era through the computer age. Today it remains one of the most theoretically important and best-respected weapons against the Grünfeld, valued for the rich, principled struggle it produces between central occupation and piece-based counterattack.

keyIdeas: 5.Qb3 regains the c4-pawn and prepares the central advance e2-e4.
White gains a broad d4/e4 centre and the space that comes with it.
Black attacks the centre with pieces, principally via ...c5 and ...b5.
The manoeuvre ...Bg4, ...Nfd7 and ...Nb6 harasses the queen and hits d4.
The exposed queen on c4 is a target Black exploits to gain tempi.
Outcome hinges on whether the white centre is a strength or a weakness.

white: Recapture on c4 with the queen and follow up with e2-e4 for a big centre.
Develop with Be2 and Be3, castle short, and post a rook on d1 to guard d4.
Consolidate the centre so the d4- and e4-pawns become a mobile asset.
Meet ...c5 and ...b5 by keeping the queen safe and holding the pawn front.
Aim to advance d4-d5 or e4-e5 once the pieces are harmoniously placed.
black: Undermine the centre with the timely breaks ...c5 and sometimes ...b5.
Play ...Bg4, ...Nfd7 and ...Nb6 to pressure d4 and chase the queen.
Choose the Hungarian ...a6 and ...b5 to gain space and hit the queen.
Exploit the long diagonal with the g7-bishop against d4 and beyond.
Liquidate or blockade the white pawns to leave the queen exposed.
